claim: The flexible N-terminal extension (NTE) of Mcm2 promotes the stable recruitment of Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) to Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
source: Using the reconstituted budding yeast DNA replication system, we find that the flexible N-terminal extension (NTE) of Mcm2 promotes the stable recruitment of Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) to Mcm2-7 double hexamers, which in turn promotes DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 and −6 and subsequent origin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the reconstituted budding yeast DNA replication system showing DDK binding to MCM DHs is dependent on the Mcm2 NTE.

claim: The Mcm2 NTE promotes DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 and Mcm6.
source: Using the reconstituted budding yeast DNA replication system, we find that the flexible N-terminal extension (NTE) of Mcm2 promotes the stable recruitment of Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) to Mcm2-7 double hexamers, which in turn promotes DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 and −6 and subsequent origin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that truncation of the Mcm2 NTE diminishes DDK-dependent phosphorylation of Mcm4 and Mcm6.

claim: The Mcm2 NTE promotes subsequent origin activation.
source: Using the reconstituted budding yeast DNA replication system, we find that the flexible N-terminal extension (NTE) of Mcm2 promotes the stable recruitment of Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) to Mcm2-7 double hexamers, which in turn promotes DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 and −6 and subsequent origin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that truncation of the Mcm2 NTE inhibits DNA replication and origin activation.

claim: The checkpoint kinase Rad53 inhibits DDK binding to Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
source: Conversely, we demonstrate that the checkpoint kinase, Rad53, inhibits DDK binding to Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Rad53 prevents DDK binding to MCM DHs.

claim: Rad53 inhibition of DDK binding to Mcm2-7 double hexamers is not dependent on Rad53 kinase activity.
source: Unexpectedly, this function is not dependent on Rad53 kinase activity, suggesting steric inhibition of DDK by activated Rad53.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that kinase-dead Rad53 can still inhibit DDK binding to MCM DHs.

claim: Activated Rad53 sterically inhibits DDK.
source: Unexpectedly, this function is not dependent on Rad53 kinase activity, suggesting steric inhibition of DDK by activated Rad53.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Rad53 inhibits DDK binding independently of its kinase activity.

claim: Bidirectional origin firing has long been recognized as a universal feature of chromosomal DNA replication in all domains of life.
source: Although bidirectional origin firing has long been recognized as a universal feature of chromosomal DNA replication in all domains of life (Huberman and Riggs, 1968; Prescott and Kuempel, 1972), how pairs of oppositely oriented replication forks are established at chromosomal origins remains poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: How pairs of oppositely oriented replication forks are established at chromosomal origins remains poorly understood.
source: Although bidirectional origin firing has long been recognized as a universal feature of chromosomal DNA replication in all domains of life (Huberman and Riggs, 1968; Prescott and Kuempel, 1972), how pairs of oppositely oriented replication forks are established at chromosomal origins remains poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Two copies of the replicative DNA helicase, Mcm2-7, are loaded as a stable double-hexameric complex around double-stranded DNA at the origin.
source: In eukaryotes, two copies of the replicative DNA helicase, Mcm2-7 (henceforth referred to as MCM), are loaded as a stable double-hexameric complex around double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) at the origin (Evrin et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2019; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MCM complex comprises six related proteins of the AAA+ family of ATPases that assemble into a hexameric ring with defined subunit order.
source: The MCM complex comprises six related proteins of the AAA+ family of ATPases that assemble into a hexameric ring with defined subunit order.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about MCM structure.

claim: The two hexamers in a MCM double hexamer associate in a head-to-head configuration.
source: Intriguingly, the two hexamers in a MCM double hexamer (DH) associate in a head-to-head configuration, thus providing a platform for the establishment of oppositely oriented sister replisomes. (Abid Ali et al., 2017; Evrin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2019; Noguchi et al., 2017; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The head-to-head configuration of MCM hexamers provides a platform for the establishment of oppositely oriented sister replisomes.

(Abid Ali et al., 2017; Evrin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2019; Noguchi et al., 2017; Remus et al., 2009).

claim: MCM DHs are catalytically inactive.
source: However, MCM DHs are catalytically inactive and require the regulated association of the essential helicase co-factors Cdc45 and GINS to form two active replicative DNA helicase complexes, termed CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS), which encircle single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) during unwinding (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MCM DHs require the regulated association of Cdc45 and GINS to form active CMG helicase complexes.
source: However, MCM DHs are catalytically inactive and require the regulated association of the essential helicase co-factors Cdc45 and GINS to form two active replicative DNA helicase complexes, termed CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS), which encircle single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) during unwinding (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CMG helicases encircle single-stranded DNA during unwinding.
source: However, MCM DHs are catalytically inactive and require the regulated association of the essential helicase co-factors Cdc45 and GINS to form two active replicative DNA helicase complexes, termed CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS), which encircle single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) during unwinding (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mechanisms must exist that ensure simultaneous progression of both helicase complexes from the origin to ensure bidirectional origin firing.
source: Therefore, to ensure bidirectional origin firing, mechanisms must exist that ensure simultaneous progression of both helicase complexes from the origin.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the requirement for bidirectional firing.

claim: An active CMG encircling ssDNA is blocked by a dsDNA-encircling inactive CMG potentially formed around the opposite MCM hexamer, thereby imposing origin bidirectionality.
source: As the head-to-head orientation of CMG helicases assembled at the origin requires them to pass each other during origin activation, it has been proposed that an active CMG encircling ssDNA is blocked by a dsDNA-encircling inactive CMG potentially formed around the opposite MCM hexamer, thereby imposing origin bidirectionality (Douglas et al., 2018; Georgescu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on a proposal from cited studies.

claim: Re-replication control is achieved by a two-step mechanism that temporally separates helicase loading in late M and G1 phase from helicase activation in S phase.
source: Such re-replication control is achieved by a two-step mechanism that temporally separates helicase loading in late M and G1 phase from helicase activation in S phase (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Helicase activation is controlled by two cell cycle-regulated protein kinases, DDK and CDK.
source: Helicase activation is controlled by two cell cycle-regulated protein kinases, Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) and cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK), which act in conjunction with a defined set of co-factors, comprising Sld3·7, Sld2, Dpb11, Pol ε, and Mcm10, in addition to GINS and Cdc45, to mediate CMG assembly (Douglas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DDK and CDK act in conjunction with Sld3·7, Sld2, Dpb11, Pol ε, Mcm10, GINS and Cdc45 to mediate CMG assembly.
source: Helicase activation is controlled by two cell cycle-regulated protein kinases, Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) and cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK), which act in conjunction with a defined set of co-factors, comprising Sld3·7, Sld2, Dpb11, Pol ε, and Mcm10, in addition to GINS and Cdc45, to mediate CMG assembly (Douglas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The essential targets of CDK during CMG assembly are Sld2 and Sld3.
source: The essential targets of CDK during CMG assembly are Sld2 and Sld3, which physically interact with distinct Dpb11 BRCT domains when phosphorylated to recruit GINS and Pol ε to the origin (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylated Sld2 and Sld3 physically interact with distinct Dpb11 BRCT domains to recruit GINS and Pol ε to the origin.
source: The essential targets of CDK during CMG assembly are Sld2 and Sld3, which physically interact with distinct Dpb11 BRCT domains when phosphorylated to recruit GINS and Pol ε to the origin (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MCM subunits are the essential targets for DDK during DNA replication.
source: Genetic and biochemical studies demonstrate that MCM subunits are the essential targets for DDK during DNA replication (Deegan et al., 2016; Hardy et al., 1997; Randell et al., 2010; Sheu and Stillman, 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of the flexible N-terminal extensions of Mcm4 and Mcm6 promotes the recruitment of Sld3·7 to MCM DHs.
source: Accordingly, DDK phosphorylation of the flexible N-terminal extensions (NTEs) of Mcm4 and −6 promotes the recruitment of Sld3·7 to MCM DHs by generating phosphorylation-dependent binding sites for Sld3, which in turn recruits Cdc45 (Deegan et al., 2016; Gros et al., 2014; Heller et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 and Mcm6 generates phosphorylation-dependent binding sites for Sld3.
source: Accordingly, DDK phosphorylation of the flexible N-terminal extensions (NTEs) of Mcm4 and −6 promotes the recruitment of Sld3·7 to MCM DHs by generating phosphorylation-dependent binding sites for Sld3, which in turn recruits Cdc45 (Deegan et al., 2016; Gros et al., 2014; Heller et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sld3 recruits Cdc45.

claim: The nature and stoichiometry of the Sld3 interaction with MCM DHs is unclear.
source: However, the nature and stoichiometry of the Sld3 interaction with MCM DHs is unclear, as Sld3 exhibits limited sequence specificity for phospho-dependent binding sites, and phospho-mimicking mutations in either Mcm4 or −6 are sufficient to bypass the requirement for DDK (Deegan et al., 2016; Randell et al., 2010).

claim: Sld3 exhibits limited sequence specificity for phospho-dependent binding sites.

claim: Replication origins do not fire simultaneously upon S phase entry, but in a staggered programmatic manner throughout S phase.
source: Replication origins do not fire simultaneously upon S phase entry, but in a staggered programmatic manner throughout S phase (Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).

claim: The replication timing program is in part imposed by limiting concentrations of the initiation factors Sld2, Dpb11, Sld3, Cdc45, and Dbf4.
source: The replication timing program is in part imposed by limiting concentrations of the initiation factors Sld2, Dpb11, Sld3, Cdc45, and Dbf4, which restrict CMG assembly to subsets of origins throughout S phase (Mantiero et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011).

claim: Limiting initiation factors are recycled from early to late origins in a normal S phase.
source: While limiting initiation factors that interact transiently with origins are thought to be recycled from early to late origins in a normal S phase, such recycling is prevented by the S phase checkpoint to inhibit late origin firing.

claim: The S phase checkpoint prevents recycling of limiting initiation factors to inhibit late origin firing.
source: While limiting initiation factors that interact transiently with origins are thought to be recycled from early to late origins in a normal S phase, such recycling is prevented by the S phase checkpoint to inhibit late origin firing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the function of the checkpoint.

claim: The S phase checkpoint induces a range of cellular responses including inhibition of origin firing, increasing dNTP levels, stabilization of stalled replication forks, and DNA repair.
source: The S phase checkpoint is a vital kinase signaling cascade that induces a range of cellular responses in addition to the inhibition of origin firing, including increasing dNTP levels, stabilization of stalled replication forks, and DNA repair to promote genome maintenance during replication stress (Pardo et al., 2017).

claim: The minimal targets for checkpoint-dependent origin inhibition in budding yeast are Sld3 and Dbf4.
source: In budding yeast, the minimal targets for checkpoint-dependent origin inhibition are Sld3 and Dbf4, which are substrates for the checkpoint effector kinase, Rad53 (Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).

source: In summary, we conclude that the Mcm2 NTE is important for DNA replication by promoting the phosphorylation of Mcm4 and −6 by DDK and subsequent CMG assembly, whereas it is dispensable for DNA replication after CMG assembly.

claim: Previous studies had proposed a docking mechanism by which a stable association of DDK with MCM DHs promotes processive multi-site phosphorylation of the Mcm4 and Mcm6 NTEs.
source: Previous studies had proposed a docking mechanism by which a stable association of DDK with MCM DHs promotes processive multi-site phosphorylation of the Mcm4 and −6 NTEs (Francis et al., 2009; Sheu and Stillman, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DDK binding to the DNA beads started to saturate at 75 nM DDK.
source: Titration of DDK into a MCM DH binding reaction revealed that DDK binding to the DNA beads started to saturate at 75 nM DDK (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When MCM DH formation was prevented by omission of Cdt1⋅MCM from the MCM loading reaction, DDK binding to the DNA beads was not observed even at 300 nM DDK.
source: Importantly, when MCM DH formation was prevented by omission of Cdt1⋅MCM from the MCM loading reaction DDK binding to the DNA beads was not observed even at 300 nM DDK, demonstrating that DDK associates with MCM DHs on the DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DDK binding assays.

claim: DDK associates with MCM DHs on the DNA.
source: Importantly, when MCM DH formation was prevented by omission of Cdt1⋅MCM from the MCM loading reaction DDK binding to the DNA beads was not observed even at 300 nM DDK, demonstrating that DDK associates with MCM DHs on the DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing DDK binding requires MCM DHs.

claim: DDK binding was exclusively observed in the presence of MCM DHs.
source: DDK binding was exclusively observed in the presence of MCM DHs; neither OCCM nor the individual loading factors ORC, Cdc6, or Cdt1⋅MCM, or pairwise combinations of these, formed stable complexes with DDK on DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DDK binding assays.

claim: Neither OCCM nor the individual loading factors ORC, Cdc6, or Cdt1⋅MCM, or pairwise combinations of these, formed stable complexes with DDK on DNA.
source: DDK binding was exclusively observed in the presence of MCM DHs; neither OCCM nor the individual loading factors ORC, Cdc6, or Cdt1⋅MCM, or pairwise combinations of these, formed stable complexes with DDK on DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DDK binding assays.

claim: DDK-MCM complex formation is strictly dependent on MCM DH assembly.
source: Thus, DDK-MCM complex formation is strictly dependent on MCM DH assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing DDK binding specificity.

claim: Truncation of the Mcm2 N-terminus resulted in severely diminished binding of DDK to MCM DHs.
source: However, truncation of the Mcm2 N-terminus resulted in severely diminished binding of DDK to MCM DHs, demonstrating that Mcm2 residues 1–127 are important for the association of DDK with MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DDK binding assays.

claim: Mcm2 residues 1–127 are important for the association of DDK with MCM DHs.
source: However, truncation of the Mcm2 N-terminus resulted in severely diminished binding of DDK to MCM DHs, demonstrating that Mcm2 residues 1–127 are important for the association of DDK with MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced DDK binding after NTE truncation.

claim: Truncation of the Mcm2 NTE prior to the addition of DDK inhibited DDK-MCM DH complex formation.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, while truncation of the Mcm2 NTE prior to the addition of DDK inhibited DDK-MCM DH complex formation as before, addition of TEV protease after DDK-MCM DH complex formation also led to the release of DDK from MCM DHs, demonstrating that the Mcm2 NTE is required for the retention of DDK on MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Addition of TEV protease after DDK-MCM DH complex formation led to the release of DDK from MCM DHs.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, while truncation of the Mcm2 NTE prior to the addition of DDK inhibited DDK-MCM DH complex formation as before, addition of TEV protease after DDK-MCM DH complex formation also led to the release of DDK from MCM DHs, demonstrating that the Mcm2 NTE is required for the retention of DDK on MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Mcm2 NTE is required for the retention of DDK on MCM DHs.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, while truncation of the Mcm2 NTE prior to the addition of DDK inhibited DDK-MCM DH complex formation as before, addition of TEV protease after DDK-MCM DH complex formation also led to the release of DDK from MCM DHs, demonstrating that the Mcm2 NTE is required for the retention of DDK on MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The DDK-MCM DH complex was remarkably resistant to extensive buffer washes including up to 0.3 M KOAc.
source: The DDK-MCM DH complex was remarkably resistant to extensive buffer washes including up to 0.3 M KOAc, attesting to the relative stability of the DDK-MCM DH interaction (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Disruption of the DDK-MCM DH complex was observed in wash buffer containing 0.5 M NaCl.
source: Disruption of the complex was observed in wash buffer containing 0.5 M NaCl, a condition in which MCM DHs remain stably bound to DNA, indicating that electrostatic interactions play an important role in mediating the DDK-MCM DH interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from salt wash experiments.

claim: Electrostatic interactions play an important role in mediating the DDK-MCM DH interaction.
source: Disruption of the complex was observed in wash buffer containing 0.5 M NaCl, a condition in which MCM DHs remain stably bound to DNA, indicating that electrostatic interactions play an important role in mediating the DDK-MCM DH interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the salt sensitivity of the DDK-MCM DH interaction.

claim: Reduced DDK binding to MCM DHs was observed in the absence of nucleotide relative to the level of DDK binding to MCM DHs in the presence of ATP, ATPγS, or AMP-PNP.
source: Indeed, reduced DDK binding to MCM DHs was observed in the absence of nucleotide relative to the level of DDK binding to MCM DHs in the presence of ATP, ATPγS, or the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue adenylyl-imidodiphosphate (AMP-PNP), indicating that ATP binding promotes DDK-MCM DH complex formation (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ATP binding promotes DDK-MCM DH complex formation.
source: Indeed, reduced DDK binding to MCM DHs was observed in the absence of nucleotide relative to the level of DDK binding to MCM DHs in the presence of ATP, ATPγS, or the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue adenylyl-imidodiphosphate (AMP-PNP), indicating that ATP binding promotes DDK-MCM DH complex formation (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The level of DDK binding to MCM DHs was essentially identical in the presence of ATP, ATPγS, or AMP-PNP.
source: Intriguingly, the level of DDK binding to MCM DHs was essentially identical in the presence of ATP, ATPγS, or AMP-PNP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from nucleotide-dependent DDK binding assays.

claim: DDK docking onto MCM DHs is independent of Mcm4 and Mcm6 phosphorylation.
source: This demonstrates that DDK docking onto MCM DHs is independent of Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that DDK binds equally well in the presence of ATP and non-hydrolyzable ATP analogues.

claim: DDK remains stably bound to the MCM DHs after phosphorylation of the Mcm4/6 NTEs.
source: Moreover, these observations reveal that DDK remains stably bound to the MCM DHs after phosphorylation of the Mcm4 /-6 NTEs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that DDK binds equally well in the presence of ATP and non-hydrolyzable ATP analogues.

claim: The Mcm2 NTE is required for the physical interaction of DDK with MCM DHs.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the Mcm2 NTE is required for the physical interaction of DDK with MCM DHs, explaining the inhibition of Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation in its absence.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: Total DNA synthesis in the complete absence of the Mcm2 residues 1–127 was reduced by ~75% relative to that in the presence of full-length Mcm2.
source: Similar to our previous approach (Figure 2), total DNA synthesis in the complete absence of the Mcm2 residues 1–127 was reduced by ~75% relative to that in the presence of full-length Mcm2 (Figure 5 A+B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The DNA synthesis defect in the absence of Mcm2 residues 1-127 was due to a defect in origin activation and not fork progression.
source: This DNA synthesis defect was due to a defect in origin activation and not fork progression as leading and lagging strand lengths were similar in both conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DNA replication was reduced by ~50% at a 1:1 ratio of Cdt1·MCM2Δ127 to wildtype Cdt1·MCM.
source: Importantly, DNA replication was reduced by ~50% at a 1:1 ratio of Cdt1·MCM2Δ127 to wildtype Cdt1·MCM, well beyond the 25% reduction expected if one Mcm2 NTE was sufficient for normal origin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mixed MCM DH experiments.

claim: The Mcm2 N-termini of both hexamers are required for efficient origin firing.
source: We conclude that the Mcm2 N-termini of both hexamers are required for efficient origin firing and that unidirectional origin firing is not supported by MCM DHs containing only a single Mcm2 NTE.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mixed MCM DH experimental data.

claim: Unidirectional origin firing is not supported by MCM DHs containing only a single Mcm2 NTE.
source: We conclude that the Mcm2 N-termini of both hexamers are required for efficient origin firing and that unidirectional origin firing is not supported by MCM DHs containing only a single Mcm2 NTE.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mixed MCM DH experimental data showing no evidence of asymmetric firing.

claim: Pre-incubation of DDK with Rad53 in the presence of ATP prior to addition of MCM DHs prevented both the binding of DDK to MCM DHs and Mcm4 and Mcm6 phosphorylation by DDK.
source: Indeed, pre-incubation of DDK with Rad53 in the presence of ATP prior to addition of MCM DHs prevented both the binding of DDK to MCM DHs and Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation by DDK (Figure 6A, lanes 4+5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rad53 was able to displace DDK from MCM DHs when DDK binding to MCM DHs preceded addition of Rad53.
source: Moreover, Rad53 was able to displace DDK from MCM DHs when DDK binding to MCM DHs preceded addition of Rad53 (lanes 4+7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sequential addition experiments.

claim: The displacement action of Rad53 was slightly less efficient at disrupting the DDK-MCM DH interaction than the action of preventing DDK recruitment.
source: However, this displacement action of Rad53 was slightly less efficient at disrupting the DDK-MCM DH interaction than the action of preventing DDK recruitment (lanes 5+7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing different orders of addition.

claim: Rad53-kd largely inhibited stable binding of DDK to MCM DHs when co-incubated with DDK prior to addition to Mcm2-7 DHs.
source: Intriguingly, Rad53-kd also largely inhibited stable binding of DDK to MCM DHs when co-incubated with DDK prior to addition to Mcm2-7 DHs, demonstrating that DDK phosphorylation by Rad53 is not essential to inhibit stable DDK recruitment to MCM (lanes 4+6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using kinase-dead Rad53.

claim: DDK phosphorylation by Rad53 is not essential to inhibit stable DDK recruitment to MCM.
source: Intriguingly, Rad53-kd also largely inhibited stable binding of DDK to MCM DHs when co-incubated with DDK prior to addition to Mcm2-7 DHs, demonstrating that DDK phosphorylation by Rad53 is not essential to inhibit stable DDK recruitment to MCM (lanes 4+6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data using kinase-dead Rad53.

claim: Some residual DDK binding and significant Mcm4 and Mcm6 phosphorylation occurred in the presence of Rad53-kd.
source: However, some residual DDK binding and significant Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation occurred in the presence of Rad53-kd, indicating that Rad53-kd-mediated inhibition of DDK is inefficient.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing incomplete inhibition by Rad53-kd.

claim: Rad53-kd-mediated inhibition of DDK is inefficient.
source: However, some residual DDK binding and significant Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation occurred in the presence of Rad53-kd, indicating that Rad53-kd-mediated inhibition of DDK is inefficient.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing incomplete inhibition by Rad53-kd.

claim: Rad53-kd was unable to displace DDK from MCM DHs when DDK was bound to MCM DHs prior to Rad53-kd addition.
source: Moreover, unlike Rad53-WT, Rad53-kd was unable to displace DDK from MCM DHs when DDK was bound to MCM DHs prior to Rad53-kd addition (lanes 4+8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sequential addition experiments.

claim: Rad53-WT efficiently inhibits origin firing in vitro both when pre-incubated with DDK or when added after DDK following MCM loading.
source: Consistent with the DDK binding data we find that Rad53-WT efficiently inhibits origin firing in vitro both when pre-incubated with DDK or when added after DDK following MCM loading (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rad53-kd was unable to inhibit origin firing when added after DDK to the replication reaction.
source: In contrast, Rad53-kd was unable to inhibit origin firing when added after DDK to the replication reaction and only partially inhibited origin firing when pre-incubated with DDK prior to addition at the MCM loading step.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA replication assays.

claim: Rad53-kd only partially inhibited origin firing when pre-incubated with DDK prior to addition at the MCM loading step.
source: In contrast, Rad53-kd was unable to inhibit origin firing when added after DDK to the replication reaction and only partially inhibited origin firing when pre-incubated with DDK prior to addition at the MCM loading step.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA replication assays.

claim: Kinase-dead alleles of Rad53 are deficient in origin inhibition.
source: These observations are consistent with genetic data demonstrating that kinase-dead alleles of Rad53 are deficient in origin inhibition (Lopes et al., 2001; Pellicioli et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Activated Rad53 inhibits DDK binding to Mcm2-7 DHs, which in turn inhibits Mcm4 and Mcm6 phosphorylation and origin activation.
source: We conclude that activated Rad53 inhibits DDK binding to Mcm2-7 DHs, which in turn inhibits Mcm4 and −6 phosphorylation and origin activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: The ability of Rad53 to prevent DDK recruitment to MCM DHs or to displace DDK from MCM DHs was undiminished in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: Strikingly, the ability of Rad53 to prevent DDK recruitment to MCM DHs or to displace DDK from MCM DHs was undiminished in the presence of AMP-PNP (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DDK phosphorylation by Rad53 is not required to control DDK-MCM DH complex formation.
source: Thus, DDK phosphorylation by Rad53 is not required to control DDK-MCM DH complex formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing Rad53 function in the presence of AMP-PNP.

claim: Rad53-WT and Rad53-kd exhibit very different elution profiles during gel-filtration chromatography.
source: Intriguingly, Rad53-WT and Rad53-kd exhibit very different elution profiles during gel-filtration chromatography (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Rad53-kd elutes at a volume that is consistent with a monomeric structure.
source: While Rad53-kd elutes at a volume that is consistent with a monomeric structure, Rad53-WT elutes as a oligomeric complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gel-filtration analysis.

claim: Rad53-WT elutes as an oligomeric complex.
source: While Rad53-kd elutes at a volume that is consistent with a monomeric structure, Rad53-WT elutes as a oligomeric complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gel-filtration analysis.

claim: Rad53 and its human homolog, Chk2, are known to associate into homo-dimeric complexes during activation by trans-autophosphorylation.
source: Rad53 and its human homolog, Chk2, are known to associate into homo-dimeric complexes during activation by trans-autophosphorylation, suggesting the oligomeric form of Rad53 observed here is a dimer (Ahn and Prives, 2002; Cai et al., 2009; Oliver et al., 2006; Wybenga-Groot et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The oligomeric form of Rad53 observed is likely a dimer.
source: Rad53 and its human homolog, Chk2, are known to associate into homo-dimeric complexes during activation by trans-autophosphorylation, suggesting the oligomeric form of Rad53 observed here is a dimer (Ahn and Prives, 2002; Cai et al., 2009; Oliver et al., 2006; Wybenga-Groot et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from citations and the gel-filtration data.

claim: Both kinase-dead Rad53 and Chk2 have been shown previously to also form dimers.
source: However, contrary to our observation, both kinase-dead Rad53 and Chk2 have been shown previously to also form dimers (Cai et al., 2009; Wybenga-Groot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rad53-WT but not Rad53-kd eluted as a stable complex with DDK during gel-filtration.
source: Importantly, Rad53-WT but not Rad53-kd eluted as a stable complex with DDK during gel-filtration (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The ability of Rad53 to bind DDK correlates with its origin inhibition function.
source: Thus, the ability of Rad53 to bind DDK correlates with its origin inhibition function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation between DDK binding and origin inhibition.

claim: Rad53 can sterically inhibit DDK binding to MCM DHs.
source: We conclude that Rad53 can sterically inhibit DDK binding to MCM DHs, suggesting a novel non-catalytic mechanism for Rad53-dependent origin control.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing kinase-independent inhibition.

claim: Simultaneous activation of both MCM hexamers at an origin is controlled by an interdependent mechanism.
source: As an alternative fail-safe mechanism, we propose that simultaneous activation of both MCM hexamers at an origin is controlled by an interdependent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the mechanism of bidirectional firing.

claim: Both Mcm2 NTEs in a MCM DH are required for tethering of a pair of DDK molecules to promote symmetric phosphorylation of both hexamers.
source: Mechanistically, we propose that both Mcm2 NTEs in a MCM DH are required for tethering of a pair of DDK molecules to promote symmetric phosphorylation of both hexamers.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the molecular mechanism.

claim: Both MCM hexamers loaded at an origin have to be physically associated to support CMG activation.
source: Supporting an interdependent hexamer activation mechanism, recent findings have demonstrated that both MCM hexamers loaded at an origin have to be physically associated to support CMG activation (Champasa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Interdependent MCM activation may conceivably be required at the origin melting step.
source: Interdependent MCM activation may conceivably be required at the origin melting step, which may involve two CMGs working in opposite direction against each other (Froelich et al., 2014; Langston and O'Donnell, 2019; Noguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations.

claim: A yeast two-hybrid study detected a specific pairwise interaction between Dbf4 and the Mcm2 N-terminus.
source: Our proposed role of the Mcm2 NTE as a DDK docking site is supported by a previous yeast two-hybrid study that detected a specific pairwise interaction between Dbf4 and the Mcm2 N-terminus (Ramer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the context of the MCM DH, the interaction between DDK and the structured NTD of Mcm4 is insufficient to tether DDK in the absence of the Mcm2 NTE.
source: Although a docking interaction between DDK and the structured NTD of Mcm4 was suggested by in vitro studies with purified DDK and Mcm4 (Sheu and Stillman, 2006), we find that in the context of the MCM DH this interaction is insufficient to tether DDK in the absence of the Mcm2 NTE.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing DDK binding requires the Mcm2 NTE.

claim: MCM DHs, but not the single MCM hexamers contained in OCCMs, are stably bound by DDK.
source: In fact, we show that MCM DHs, but not the single MCM hexamers contained in OCCMs, are stably bound by DDK (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MCM DHs are preferred phosphorylation targets for DDK over single MCM hexamers.
source: This is consistent with previous data demonstrating that MCM DHs are preferred phosphorylation targets for DDK over single MCM hexamers (Francis et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prior phosphorylation of MCM by other kinases has been shown to promote DDK binding to MCM at origins.
source: Moreover, prior phosphorylation of MCM by other kinases has also been shown to promote DDK binding to MCM at origins (Francis et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: ATP-binding promotes DDK-MCM complex formation.
source: In addition, we show that ATP-binding promotes DDK-MCM complex formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from nucleotide-dependent binding assays.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of MCM is opposed by dephosphorylation of MCM by the Rif1-PP1 phosphatase complex.
source: DDK phosphorylation of MCM is opposed by dephosphorylation of MCM by the Rif1-PP1 phosphatase complex (Alver et al., 2017; Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017; Mattarocci et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tethering of DDK to MCM DHs is likely to promote MCM phosphorylation in vivo by shifting the balance between DDK and Rif1-PP1 activity toward DDK.
source: While tethering of DDK to MCM DHs may, therefore, not be essential for maintaining DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4/6 in the absence of Rif1-PP1 in vitro (Figure 3B, lane six and Figure 4C, lane 4), it is likely to promote MCM phosphorylation in vivo by shifting the balance between DDK and Rif1-PP1 activity toward DDK.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the in vivo function.

claim: Retention of DDK at early origins until origin firing may prevent premature recycling of DDK to late origins to establish the replication timing program.
source: Additionally, as Dbf4 concentrations are limiting for origin activation, retention of DDK at early origins until origin firing may prevent premature recycling of DDK to late origins to establish the replication timing program (Mantiero et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations.

claim: Retention of DDK at unfired origins has been proposed to restrict DDK targeting of Eco1 until late S phase to control cohesion in the cell cycle.
source: Similarly, retention of DDK at unfired origins has been proposed to restrict DDK targeting of Eco1 until late S phase to control cohesion in the cell cycle (Seoane and Morgan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DDK release from MCM DHs is regulated by origin activation.
source: These mechanisms imply that DDK release from MCM DHs is regulated by origin activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanisms.

claim: The association of DDK with replisomes was shown to link DNA replication with meiotic recombination.
source: Indeed, the association of DDK with replisomes was shown to link DNA replication with meiotic recombination (Murakami and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Dbf4 contains three evolutionarily conserved sequence motifs, termed N, M, and C that constitute parts of distinct domains separated by flexible linkers.
source: Dbf4 contains three evolutionarily conserved sequence motifs, termed N, M, and C that constitute parts of distinct domains separated by flexible linkers (Hughes et al., 2012; Masai and Arai, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The M and C domains of Dbf4 embrace the Cdc7 kinase to mediate Cdc7 activation.
source: The M and C domains embrace the Cdc7 kinase to mediate Cdc7 activation, while the N motif forms part of an N-terminal BRCT domain that is dispensable for Cdc7 activation (Almawi et al., 2016; Dick et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The N motif of Dbf4 forms part of an N-terminal BRCT domain that is dispensable for Cdc7 activation.
source: The M and C domains embrace the Cdc7 kinase to mediate Cdc7 activation, while the N motif forms part of an N-terminal BRCT domain that is dispensable for Cdc7 activation (Almawi et al., 2016; Dick et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An N-terminal fragment of Dbf4 encompassing the BRCT and M domains is required and sufficient to target Dbf4 to MCM complexes loaded at replication origins.
source: Intriguingly, an N-terminal fragment encompassing the BRCT and M domains is required and sufficient to target Dbf4 to MCM complexes loaded at replication origins (Dowell et al., 1994; Francis et al., 2009), while a physical interaction between Rad53 and the Dbf4 BRCT domain has been proposed to contribute to checkpoint-dependent origin control (Chen et al., 2013; Duncker et al., 2002; Matthews et al., 2012; Matthews et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A physical interaction between Rad53 and the Dbf4 BRCT domain has been proposed to contribute to checkpoint-dependent origin control.
source: Intriguingly, an N-terminal fragment encompassing the BRCT and M domains is required and sufficient to target Dbf4 to MCM complexes loaded at replication origins (Dowell et al., 1994; Francis et al., 2009), while a physical interaction between Rad53 and the Dbf4 BRCT domain has been proposed to contribute to checkpoint-dependent origin control (Chen et al., 2013; Duncker et al., 2002; Matthews et al., 2012; Matthews et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Competitive binding of Rad53 to the Dbf4 BRCT domain is likely in part responsible for the inhibition of DDK binding to MCM DHs.
source: Thus, competitive binding of Rad53 to the Dbf4 BRCT domain is likely in part responsible for the inhibition of DDK binding to MCM DHs observed here.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known interactions and experimental data.

claim: The N-terminal region of Dbf4 has been shown to interact with ORC.
source: The N-terminal region of Dbf4 has also been shown to interact with ORC (Duncker et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Purified MCM DHs can recruit DDK to replication origins independently of ORC.
source: However, consistent with a previous study in whole-cell yeast extracts (Francis et al., 2009), we show here that purified MCM DHs can recruit DDK to replication origins independently of ORC and, conversely, that ORC alone is incapable of recruiting DDK to DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to a previous study.

claim: ORC alone is incapable of recruiting DDK to DNA.
source: However, consistent with a previous study in whole-cell yeast extracts (Francis et al., 2009), we show here that purified MCM DHs can recruit DDK to replication origins independently of ORC and, conversely, that ORC alone is incapable of recruiting DDK to DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to a previous study.

claim: The oligomeric state of Rad53, the Rad53 phosphorylation state, or both control the ability of Rad53 to displace DDK from MCM DHs.
source: However, as Rad53-dependent DDK displacement from MCM DHs does not require Rad53 kinase activity, we suggest that the oligomeric state of Rad53, the Rad53 phosphorylation state, or both control the ability of Rad53 to displace DDK from MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the experimental observations.

claim: Active Rad53-wt forms oligomers, likely dimers, in solution.
source: While Rad53-kd is monomeric in solution, we show that active Rad53-wt forms oligomers, likely dimers, in solution.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gel-filtration analysis.

claim: Following recruitment to MCM DHs, DDK may form a dimer on the MCM DH surface that is in complex with both Mcm2 NTEs.
source: We propose that following recruitment to MCM DHs, DDK may form a dimer on the MCM DH surface that is in complex with both Mcm2 NTEs, which we show are required for maintaining DDK at MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the experimental data.

claim: A DDK dimer bound to a MCM DH may require simultaneous disruption of the interaction of both DDK molecules with MCM for DDK release.
source: A DDK dimer bound to a MCM DH may require simultaneous disruption of the interaction of both DDK molecules with MCM for DDK release, explaining the proficiency of dimeric Rad53-WT and, conversely, deficiency of monomeric Rad53-kd to compete DDK off MCM DHs.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Following DDK displacement, PP1 would be able to dephosphorylate the Mcm4 and Mcm6 NTEs and thus inactivate the origin.
source: Following DDK displacement, PP1 would then be able to dephosphorylate the Mcm4 and −6 NTEs and thus inactivate the origin.
